texts.title: The Study That Checked the Studies

task.en: Read and find out: what proportion of the hundred studies produced the same result when repeated?
task.ru: Прочитайте и узнайте: какая доля из ста исследований дала тот же результат при повторении?
task.kz: Оқып, біліңіз: жүз зерттеудің қанша бөлігі қайталанғанда сол нәтижені берді?

words.ex: A finding that cannot be replicated is not yet knowledge.
All hundred studies had appeared in peer-reviewed journals.
Only 36 per cent of the repeated experiments produced a statistically significant result.
The incentives of academic life reward novelty, not verification.
Analytical flexibility allows researchers to find patterns in noise.
Researchers now preregister their hypotheses before collecting data.
Science is supposed to be self-correcting.
The episode has taught the field a certain humility.

text: In August 2015 the journal Science published a paper with 270 authors and a deceptively modest title: “Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science.” Behind it lay four years of work by a loose network of researchers who had done something that almost nobody in their profession does: instead of running new experiments, they had gone back and repeated old ones. They chose one hundred studies, all published in three leading peer-reviewed journals in 2008, and attempted, as faithfully as they could, to reproduce them. The results made headlines around the world, and not because they were reassuring.

Of the original hundred studies, ninety-seven had reported a statistically significant effect — the conventional threshold at which a result is considered real rather than accidental. When the experiments were repeated, only thirty-six did. Where effects did appear, they were on average about half as large as first claimed. Well-known findings crumbled: the idea that adopting a “power pose” for two minutes changes your hormones and your confidence; the claim that willpower is a limited resource which runs out like fuel; the suggestion that reading a passage about old age makes people walk more slowly down a corridor. Each had been cited hundreds of times, taught in textbooks and repeated in bestselling books. None survived intact.

The paper did not accuse anyone of fraud, and fraud, in fact, is the least of the problem. What it exposed was something more ordinary and therefore more troubling: a set of incentives that quietly push honest people towards unreliable conclusions. Academic careers are built on publications, journals prefer novel and positive results, and a study that finds nothing is nearly impossible to publish. Under those conditions, researchers acquire a great deal of what statisticians politely call “analytical flexibility.” They can stop collecting data as soon as the numbers look favourable, test a dozen variables and report the one that worked, or quietly drop the participants who spoil the pattern. None of this feels like cheating from the inside. Each decision is defensible on its own. Together, they allow a scientist to find a signal in pure noise — and to believe it.

The problem, it soon became clear, was not confined to psychology. Similar exercises in cancer biology, economics and medicine produced comparable figures, and in 2016 a survey of 1,500 scientists found that more than half had failed to reproduce their own results at least once. The phrase “replication crisis” entered the language, and with it an uncomfortable question: if a large fraction of the published literature could not be trusted, what exactly had the previous decades of research established?

The response has been, by the standards of academic culture, remarkably fast. Thousands of researchers now preregister their studies — that is, they publish their hypotheses, sample sizes and methods of analysis before collecting a single data point, so that the flexibility described above is no longer available to them. Journals have begun to accept papers on the basis of the question and the design, rather than the result, which removes the pressure to produce a positive finding. Raw data and computer code, once jealously guarded, are increasingly shared by default. Several of the researchers whose famous findings failed to replicate have publicly acknowledged the fact — an act that, a generation earlier, would have been almost unthinkable.

It would be easy to read all this as a story about the failure of science. It is more accurately a story about science doing, slowly and painfully, what it is supposed to do. A finding that has been published is not yet knowledge; it is a claim, and claims must survive attempts to destroy them. For decades the attempts were simply not being made, because nobody was rewarded for making them. The 2015 project was, in a sense, the field remembering its own rules.

The episode has left the discipline with a certain humility, and perhaps with a better sense of what a single study can and cannot show. The next time a headline announces that scientists have proved something surprising about human nature, the appropriate response is neither belief nor cynicism, but a question that the 270 authors would recognise: has anyone tried it twice?

text: On 14 December 1912, three men and two sledges were crossing a plateau of ice some three hundred miles east of their base in Antarctica. Douglas Mawson, the leader of the Australasian Antarctic Expedition, was walking beside the first sledge. Xavier Mertz, a Swiss lawyer and champion skier, was ahead on skis. Belgrave Ninnis, a young British army officer, was with the second sledge, which carried the tent, most of the food, and the six strongest dogs. Mertz raised a ski pole to signal a crevasse; Mawson crossed it without difficulty. When he looked back a minute later, the second sledge was gone. So were the dogs, and so was Ninnis. Where they had been there was a hole in the snow. They called into the crevasse for three hours.

The two survivors took stock. They had one sledge, a spare tent cover but no tent, six weak dogs, and food for about a week. The base was three hundred miles away. There was no radio and no possibility of rescue; the ship that was to collect the expedition would leave in mid-January. The arithmetic was simple and unforgiving: they would have to walk home on far fewer calories than the journey required, and they would have to eat the dogs.

They did, one by one, boiling the meat and, because nothing could be wasted, the livers. Neither man could have known what modern medicine established decades later: the liver of a sled dog contains such a concentration of vitamin A that a single portion is toxic to a human being. Within two weeks both men were losing skin from their faces and hands. Mertz, who ate more of the liver because he found the muscle harder to chew, deteriorated with frightening speed. He became confused, then violent, then still. On 8 January 1913 he died in the tent, and Mawson, himself so weak that he could barely stand, buried him in the snow and read a service over the grave.

He was now alone, a hundred miles from the base, with a sledge he could hardly pull. He cut it in half with a pocket knife to lighten it. When he took off his boots to examine his feet, he found that the soles had separated from the flesh beneath them and were lying loose in his socks. He bandaged them back into place, put on six pairs of socks, and walked.

On 17 January the surface gave way and he fell into a crevasse. The sledge caught on the lip above him, and he found himself hanging in his harness over a drop with no visible bottom, at the end of fourteen feet of rope. He would later write that his first thought was relief: it would be a quick end. Then he thought of the food still on the sledge, and it seemed absurd to die with food uneaten. He climbed the rope, hand over hand, with fingers that had no skin. At the top the lip collapsed and he fell the full length again. He hung there, he said, for some time, and then climbed once more, and lay on the surface for an hour before he could move.

He reached the base on 8 February, thirty days after Mertz's death, and a few hours after the ship had sailed. Six men had been left behind to search for him, and one of them, seeing a figure approaching across the ice, could not tell which of the three it was. Radio contact with the ship was made, but a storm prevented it from returning, and Mawson spent another year in Antarctica before he could go home.

Physiologists have since calculated that he should not have survived: the combination of starvation, vitamin poisoning, cold and injury exceeded what the human body is understood to tolerate. Mawson himself offered no theory beyond the obvious one. He kept walking because stopping seemed, on balance, the worse option. He lived to be seventy-six, and the account he wrote of the journey, published in 1915, ends not with triumph but with a list of the men who did not come back.

texts.title: The Tent Cut From the Inside

words.ex: The tent was pitched on a slope that seemed too gentle for an avalanche.
Some of the hikers had left the tent barefoot in minus thirty.
The autopsies revealed injuries that no fall could explain.
A slab avalanche can be small, silent and deadly.
For sixty years no explanation seemed entirely plausible.
Conspiracy theories filled the gap that the evidence left.
Their computer simulation reproduced the injuries exactly.
Whether the mystery is finally resolved depends on whom you ask.

text: On 1 February 1959, nine experienced hikers — seven men and two women, pitched their tent on the eastern slope of a mountain the local Mansi people called Kholat Syakhl, “Dead Mountain”. They were on a sixteen-day ski trek in the northern Urals, and the photographs they left behind show a cheerful, competent group making camp at about five in the afternoon. Nobody saw them alive again.

When a search party reached the site three weeks later, they found the tent half-buried and empty. It had been cut open from the inside. Leading away from it, down the slope towards a forest a mile and a half below, were the footprints of eight or nine people, some in socks, some in a single boot, some barefoot. The temperature that night had been around minus thirty. Under a cedar tree at the edge of the forest the searchers found the remains of a small fire and the first two bodies, dressed only in underwear. The last four were not found until May, when the snow melted, in a ravine under four metres of snow.

It was the autopsies that turned a tragedy into a mystery. Six of the nine had died of hypothermia, which was terrible but explicable. The other three had injuries that were not: one had a fractured skull, and two had massive chest fractures of the kind, the examining doctor said, that he would expect from a car crash — yet there were no external wounds, no bruising to suggest a fight, and no sign of any other people in the area. One woman was missing her tongue. Some of the clothes showed traces of radioactivity. The official inquiry concluded that the group had died as a result of “a compelling natural force”, and closed the file.

Into the silence flowed every theory that a cold war could produce. Secret weapons tests, escaped prisoners, infrasound, aliens. The Soviet authorities' reluctance to release documents guaranteed that each theory survived, and by the time the archives were partly opened in the 1990s the Dyatlov Pass incident — named after the group's twenty-three-year-old leader, Igor Dyatlov — had become one of the most famous unsolved cases in the world, the subject of films and books.

The obvious answer, an avalanche, had always seemed impossible. The slope was too gentle, at less than thirty degrees; there was no debris; the tent was still standing; and the searchers had found no sign of a slide. Then, in 2019, a Russian prosecutor's office reopened the case and concluded that an avalanche was, after all, the cause — a verdict that satisfied almost nobody, since it did not explain how.

The explanation came from an unexpected direction. Johan Gaume, a Swiss avalanche scientist, and Alexander Puzrin, a geotechnical engineer at ETH Zurich, took the problem apart with computer models of snow and the human body — including, memorably, an animation engine that had been developed for the Disney film “Frozen”. Their paper, published in 2021, showed that the hikers had made one fatal decision: to cut into the slope to level a platform for the tent. That cut weakened the base of a slab of hard, wind-packed snow above them. Hours later, as the wind loaded more snow onto the slope, the slab released — a small, slow, almost silent block, perhaps five metres long, sliding a few metres onto the tent. It would also, the simulations showed, have produced exactly the chest and skull fractures the doctor had described, because the hikers were lying on stiff ski bases rather than soft ground. Half-crushed and terrified, the survivors cut their way out and fled downhill.

Not everyone accepts the account; the missing tongue and the radioactivity, in particular, still attract attention, though both have mundane explanations involving scavengers and the lantern mantles of the period. But for the first time in sixty years, the physics and the evidence agree. Puzrin has said that the most convincing part, to him, was the simplest: nine people, in the dark, trying to help each other down a mountain. That is not a mystery. That is what people do.

text: In the summer of 1889, a Russian explorer named Nikolai Yadrintsev was travelling through the valley of the Orkhon river in northern Mongolia when he came upon two tall stone monuments standing among the ruins of an ancient city. Each was covered, on all four sides, with dense columns of angular letters that nobody in his party could read. One stone also carried a text in Chinese. Yadrintsev made careful copies and sent them to Europe, where they caused a sensation among scholars — and a certain amount of embarrassment, because the letters resembled the runes of medieval Scandinavia and a number of learned people were quick to announce that the Vikings had reached Mongolia.

Similar inscriptions had in fact been known for almost two centuries. Swedish prisoners of war, sent to Siberia after their defeat by Peter the Great in 1709, had reported stones covered in strange writing along the Yenisei river. But the Yenisei stones were short and worn. The Orkhon monuments were long — one carried over sixty lines — and the Chinese text offered, for the first time, a possible key. Two expeditions, one Finnish and one Russian, hurried to Mongolia in 1890 and 1891 to make proper rubbings.

It was won, with astonishing speed, by a Danish philologist named Vilhelm Thomsen, who had never been to Mongolia. He began with the Chinese text, which named the man for whom the monument had been raised: a prince called Kul Tigin, who had died in 731. Thomsen then looked for the same name in the unknown script. He also assumed, correctly, that a monument of this kind would contain the words for “sky” or “god” — tengri — and the title khagan. With three words fixed, he could begin to assign sounds to signs. On 15 December 1893 he presented his alphabet to the Royal Danish Academy. The language, he announced, was Turkic — an ancestor of Kazakh and other Turkic languages — and the script, despite appearances, had nothing whatever to do with Vikings.

What the stones said turned out to be more remarkable than the fact that they could be read at all. The larger monument, raised in 732 by the khagan Bilge for his younger brother Kul Tigin, is an account of the Second Turkic Khaganate told in the first person: how the Turks had once lost their independence to China, how they had regained it. It is part history, part lament and part political warning. “When the blue sky above and the brown earth below were created,” it begins, “between the two were created the sons of men.” Later it addresses its readers directly: the Turkic people, it says, were seduced by the “soft words and fine silk” of a foreign power and nearly disappeared as a nation. A second stone, for Bilge himself, followed in 735; a third, older one commemorates the counsellor Tonyukuk and was, unusually, written while its subject was still alive.

For linguists, the inscriptions are a foundation stone. They are the oldest substantial texts in any Turkic language, and much of what is known about how those languages developed rests on them. The script itself — now generally called Old Turkic rather than runic — is a sophisticated instrument: it uses separate consonant signs depending on whether the neighbouring vowel is front or back.

For the modern Turkic nations the stones have a different meaning. In Kazakhstan, the Kul Tigin text is quoted on monuments and in school textbooks; a full-size copy of the stone stands in the Eurasian National University in Astana. A monument raised thirteen centuries ago to warn one people against forgetting themselves has become, for their distant descendants, a way of remembering.

Thomsen lived until 1927 and worked on the inscriptions for the rest of his life. He never saw the stones. They still stand where Yadrintsev found them, in the wind of the Orkhon valley, under a roof that was built in 2010 to protect them. Their letters, once unreadable, are now taught to schoolchildren three thousand kilometres away.

text: In the spring of 1900, a boat carrying Greek sponge divers took shelter from a storm beside the small island of Antikythera, between Crete and the Peloponnese. When the weather cleared, one of the divers went down to look for sponges and came up babbling about a heap of dead horses and naked people on the sea floor. What he had found, at a depth of about forty-five metres, was a Roman-era shipwreck full of bronze and marble statues. Over the following year, in the first large underwater excavation in history, the divers brought up dozens of them. They also brought up, almost incidentally, a lump of corroded bronze the size of a large book, which was placed in a corner of the National Archaeological Museum in Athens and largely ignored.

In 1902 an archaeologist noticed that the lump had split, and that inside it there was a gear wheel. This made no sense. Gears of that precision were thought to belong to the fourteenth century, when European clockmakers began to build astronomical clocks; the ship had sunk in about 60 BC. It was not until the 1950s that a British physicist, Derek de Solla Price, began the slow work of taking it seriously, and not until 1971 that X-rays gave him a first look inside.

What the X-rays showed, and what a far more powerful examination confirmed in 2006, was a machine. At least thirty interlocking bronze gears, some with teeth barely a millimetre long, had once been fitted into a wooden case about the size of a shoebox. A handle on the side turned them all. On the front, pointers moved across a dial showing the zodiac and the Egyptian calendar; on the back, two spiral dials tracked the Moon and predicted eclipses. One small gear, mounted off-centre on another, reproduced the Moon's variable speed across the sky. Inscriptions on the case, only readable through X-ray tomography, turned out to be a user's manual.

It was, in short, an analogue computer. Turn the handle to a date, and the mechanism would tell you the position of the Sun and Moon, the phase of the Moon, the timing of the next eclipse, the year of the next Olympic Games and, according to the most recent reconstructions, the positions of the five planets known to the ancient world. Nothing remotely as sophisticated survives from the following thousand years.

Who built it, and where, remains unknown. The inscriptions are in Greek, and some of the astronomical details point to Rhodes or to Corinth; the workmanship is so assured that it can hardly have been the maker's first attempt, which means there were others. Cicero, writing in the first century BC, describes similar devices built by Archimedes and by the philosopher Posidonius, and for a long time historians assumed he was exaggerating. He was not. What is remarkable is not that the Greeks could build such a thing, but that the knowledge disappeared so completely. The technology had to be invented all over again in medieval Europe.

Teams at University College London have built working reconstructions; a 2021 paper reconstructed the front dial from the surviving fragments and the inscriptions alone. Divers with modern equipment have returned to the wreck several times since 2012 and have found, among other things, a bronze arm, a human skeleton and further fragments of bronze that may or may not belong to the device. About a third of the original mechanism has been recovered. The rest is presumably still on the sea floor, forty-five metres down, waiting.

There is a lesson in the object that has nothing to do with gears. For over half a century it sat in a museum, labelled and catalogued, and nobody looked at it properly, because everybody knew that such a thing could not exist. The Antikythera mechanism is an anomaly, and anomalies are uncomfortable; the easiest way to deal with them is to file them in a corner. The sponge diver who found the wreck was told, at first, that he had been hallucinating.

text: For a few weeks each April, the foothills between Shymkent and the Tien Shan mountains turn red. A wild, patchy scarlet runs across whole hillsides and stops at the edge of the snow. These are Greig's tulips, Tulipa greigii, growing where they have always grown. Most visitors who photograph them do not know that they are looking at the origin of one of the most valuable plants in human history — or that the Dutch, who sell three billion tulip bulbs a year, are selling the descendants of these hills.

The tulip is a Central Asian plant. Of the roughly seventy-five wild species known to botanists, more than half grow in the mountains and steppes of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and the surrounding region, and Kazakhstan alone is home to around thirty-five, several of them endemic — found nowhere else on Earth. They evolved for a hard climate: a bulb that sleeps through summer and winter, then races to flower in the brief, wet spring. The flower's cup shape, which gardeners prize, is a device for catching warmth; on a cold morning the inside of a tulip can be several degrees warmer than the air.

The Persians and later the Ottomans grew them in gardens, but it was in Istanbul in the sixteenth century that the tulip became an obsession. Sultans planted them by the hundred thousand; the lâle, as it was called, appeared on tiles, textiles and armour. In the 1550s the Habsburg ambassador to the Ottoman court, Ogier de Busbecq, sent bulbs and seeds westward, and by the 1590s the botanist Carolus Clusius was cultivating them in the university garden at Leiden, in the Netherlands. When some of his bulbs were stolen, the thieves unwittingly founded an industry.

The Dutch soil suited the plant, and Dutch merchants suited the trade. By the 1630s rare varieties — especially those with flames and feathers of colour, which we now know were caused by a virus — were changing hands for astonishing sums. In February 1637 a single bulb of the variety Semper Augustus was reportedly offered for the price of a good house on an Amsterdam canal. The market collapsed within a week. “Tulip mania” has been cited ever since as the first speculative bubble in history, though modern historians argue that its scale was exaggerated by moralists at the time; most of the trading was done by a small circle of wealthy amateurs, and few people were actually ruined.

What is not exaggerated is the plant's subsequent conquest of the world. The Netherlands today grows tulips on about ten thousand hectares and exports them to every continent, and the flower has become so thoroughly Dutch in the popular imagination that its Asian origin surprises most people. Genetic studies have confirmed what botanists suspected: the garden tulip is largely descended from a small number of Central Asian species, Tulipa greigii and Tulipa kaufmanniana among them — the very flowers on the hills above Shymkent.

Those hills are not as safe as they look. Wild tulips face three threats, all of them ordinary. Overgrazing by sheep and cattle strips the hillsides before the plants can set seed. Illegal collectors dig up bulbs to sell, and picnickers pick the flowers by the armful. And the land itself is being ploughed, built on or, increasingly, dried out by a changing climate. Several Kazakh species are listed in the country's Red Book of threatened plants, and one, the tulip of the Karatau mountains, exists in only a handful of locations.

There is a certain irony in a country that gave the world its most popular flower having to campaign to protect the flower at home. Kazakhstan has begun to do so: nature reserves have been expanded, an annual tulip festival near Shymkent now draws thousands of visitors who are asked to look rather than pick, and botanists have proposed the wild tulip as a national symbol. Whether the red hillsides survive the next century will depend less on Dutch greenhouses than on Kazakh shepherds — and on whether the visitors with cameras remember, when they leave, to take only pictures.

words.ex: The manuscripts covered astronomy, law, medicine and poetry.
In 2012 militants took control of the city.
The trunks were smuggled out by donkey cart, boat and bus.
Every road out of the city had a checkpoint.
Timbuktu was once a centre of Islamic scholarship.

text: The city of Timbuktu, on the southern edge of the Sahara in Mali, has been a byword for remoteness for so long that many people assume it is imaginary. It is not. In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries it was one of the great centres of learning in the Islamic world, with a university, dozens of schools and a trade in books that was said to be more profitable than the trade in gold. The scholars who lived there wrote, copied and collected manuscripts on astronomy, mathematics, law, medicine, music and poetry, and when the city declined, the books did not disappear. Families buried them in the desert, walled them into houses and hid them in caves, and passed the secret from father to son for four hundred years.

Abdel Kader Haidara grew up in one of those families. When his father died in 1981, the seventeen-year-old inherited a library of several thousand manuscripts and, with it, a responsibility he did not want. He was persuaded to work for a state institute that was trying to collect the city's scattered books, and he spent the next decade travelling by camel and canoe to villages along the Niger river. By the early 2000s, with foreign funding, he and other families had built more than forty private libraries in Timbuktu, and the total number of manuscripts in the city was estimated at nearly 400,000.

In April 2012 the arrangement collapsed. Militants allied to al-Qaeda seized the north of Mali, including Timbuktu, and began to impose their version of religious law. Music was banned, shrines were destroyed, and it was clear to Haidara that the manuscripts — many of which contained ideas the militants considered heretical — would be next. So he decided to make the books disappear again.

The operation that followed was carried out by librarians, students, shopkeepers and teenagers. First, they bought every metal footlocker in the markets of Timbuktu and the surrounding towns — some 2,500 of them — and, working at night, packed the manuscripts into them. The trunks were moved in small numbers to private homes across the city so that no single raid could find them all. Then, over the course of several months, they were carried out: by donkey cart to the river, by boat down the Niger, by bus and four-wheel drive along roads with a checkpoint every few kilometres. Couriers, some of them teenage boys and girls, kept their eyes down. At least one convoy was stopped, searched and, after a long conversation, allowed to pass. Others were saved by bribes, by luck, or by the sheer improbability of the cargo.

By the time French and Malian forces retook Timbuktu in January 2013, about 350,000 manuscripts had been moved to the capital, Bamako, a thousand kilometres to the south. The militants, retreating, set fire to the one library whose contents had been left behind. Of the 4,000 manuscripts in it, most had already been quietly removed. A few hundred burned.

Rescue, it turned out, was only the first problem. Bamako lies in a wetter climate than the desert city, and paper that had survived five centuries in dry air began, within months, to grow mould. Haidara's organisation raised money for dehumidifiers, archival boxes and a team of conservators, and began the long task of cataloguing and digitising a collection that had never been fully catalogued in the first place. Scholars who now read the digitised pages are finding treatises on conflict resolution, arguments against slavery, and observations of the stars.

Haidara is reluctant to be called a hero, partly because so many people took the same risks, and partly because the manuscripts are not yet home. Most are still in Bamako. The plan, he says, is to return them to Timbuktu when it is safe, to the families and the libraries they came from — which is to say, to do what his ancestors did, in reverse. In the meantime, the books are exactly where his father would have understood them to be: hidden, cared for, and waiting.

words.ex: The walls are lattice sections called kerege.
The yurt is a dwelling designed to be taken apart.
Layers of felt keep out both frost and heat.
Felt is a remarkable natural insulation.
The etiquette of the yurt governs where each guest sits.
The hearth stands at the centre, under the shanyrak.
UNESCO lists yurt-making as intangible cultural heritage.
A family can assemble a yurt in about an hour.

text: A yurt has no corners, no nails and no foundations, and it can be taken down, loaded onto two camels and put up again fifty kilometres away by the same afternoon. But to describe the yurt as a tent is to miss what it is. It is a building with a grammar — a set of rules about structure, direction and behaviour — and reading that grammar tells you a good deal about the culture that produced it.

Start with the structure. The walls are made of kerege, sections of wooden lattice that fold flat for transport and open into a circle. From the top of the walls rise the uyk, long curved poles, each fitted at its upper end into a hole in the shanyrak: the wooden ring that crowns the whole and holds it in tension. Nothing is fixed; everything leans on everything else. Over this skeleton go layers of felt, made by beating and rolling sheep's wool until the fibres lock together — a material that keeps out frost and heat, and that breathes, so the air inside never becomes stale. A skilled family can assemble the whole thing in about an hour. The largest ceremonial yurts, with twelve or more kerege sections, are the size of a small hall.

Now the direction. The door faces east, or slightly south of east. Inside, the space is mapped. Directly opposite the door is the tor, the place of honour, where the most respected guest sits on a pile of the best carpets. The right-hand side, as you enter, belonged traditionally to the women and the household; the left to the men, their saddles and their weapons. In the centre, under the shanyrak, is the hearth, and the shanyrak's opening above it lets out the smoke and lets in the light, so that the ring functions as chimney, window and clock: the sunbeam that falls through it moves across the interior during the day, and a household could tell the hour from where it fell.

The etiquette follows from the map. A guest does not step on the threshold, does not walk between the hearth and the tor, and does not sit in the tor uninvited. Much of this survives in Kazakh homes that have never been round: the seating of an honoured guest opposite the door. The house has changed shape; the grammar has not.

Of all the parts, the shanyrak carries the most meaning. It is the one component that is not replaced. Kerege break, felt wears out, uyk are cut new from willow, but the ring at the top is passed from father to youngest son, and to inherit it is to inherit the household itself. The phrase for founding a family is “to raise a shanyrak”. The ring appears at the centre of the state emblem of Kazakhstan, with the uyk radiating from it like sunbeams — a nation, the design suggests, is a single dwelling with a single hearth.

The yurt is not a museum piece. In the west and south of the country, herding families still spend the summer in them; in the cities, they appear on public squares for Nauryz, at weddings and at funerals, where the mourning is held under felt as it has been for a thousand years. A small industry of makers survives, mostly in Kyzylorda and Turkistan regions, and in 2014 UNESCO added the craft of the Kazakh and Kyrgyz yurt to its list of intangible cultural heritage.

What the yurt ultimately expresses is a particular idea of home: not a place, but a structure that can be carried, and a set of relationships that it holds in tension the way the shanyrak holds the poles. A house that cannot move belongs to the land. A yurt belongs to the family. Take it down, fold the walls, load the camels — and the home goes with you, complete, to wherever the grass is next.

words.ex: The perception of time is not a clock but a construction.
A year is proportionally smaller for a fifty-year-old than for a child.
Novelty stretches time in memory.
In retrospect, a dull week seems to have taken no time at all.
The brain encodes new experiences in far more detail.
Dopamine levels influence how fast the internal clock runs.
Routine is the great compressor of time.
You can deliberately slow your years down.

text: Ask almost anyone over forty and you will hear the same complaint: the years are speeding up. Summer holidays that once lasted an eternity now seem to end before they have begun. The experience is so universal that it has been remarked on for at least two thousand years, and yet it is only recently that psychologists and neuroscientists have begun to take it apart. What they have found is that the feeling is real — and that it has less to do with the clock than with the way memory is built.

The oldest explanation is arithmetical. In 1877 the French philosopher Paul Janet proposed that we judge the length of a period of time in proportion to the time we have already lived. To a five-year-old, a year is a fifth of everything; to a fifty-year-old, it is a fiftieth, and it should therefore feel ten times shorter. The theory is elegant. But it has problems. It predicts that time should speed up smoothly and continuously, whereas most people report that the acceleration is uneven — a slow adolescence, a blur in the thirties, and, oddly, a partial slowing again in old age.

A second account looks at memory rather than mathematics. A week of holiday in an unfamiliar city seems to fly past while you are living it, yet in retrospect it feels enormously long, packed with incident; a week of ordinary work drags by hour after hour and then, looked back on, vanishes almost entirely. The explanation is that we estimate the duration of past time from the number of distinct memories it contains. Novelty forces the brain to encode experience in detail and a period rich in such memories seems long. Routine, by contrast, is compressed: the brain files a hundred similar mornings as one. And routine is precisely what adult life accumulates. The child's year is a sequence of firsts; the adult's is, increasingly, a sequence of repeats.

There is physiological support for this. Brain imaging shows that the hippocampus, which lays down new memories, responds most strongly to unfamiliar information and grows quiet as experiences become predictable. The neurotransmitter dopamine, which is involved in both novelty and the sense of time passing, declines gradually from early adulthood. In 2019 an engineer at Duke University, Adrian Bejan, added a physical argument: the speed at which the brain processes images slows as neural pathways lengthen and degrade with age, so that an adult receives fewer distinct “frames” per second than a child, and a day with fewer frames in it feels shorter. The idea is contested, but it points in the same direction as the memory research: subjective time is not measured, it is counted, and the units are events.

None of these theories is complete, and they are not mutually exclusive. What they share is a conclusion that turns the problem around. If the years feel short because they contain few distinct memories, then the sensation is not an inevitable feature of ageing but a side effect of how an adult typically lives. The speeding up of time is, in that reading, a symptom of a life that has stopped generating novelty.

The practical implication follows directly, and it is more cheerful than the diagnosis. Time can be slowed, at least in memory, by doing what the brain is built to notice: learning a language, taking a different route, travelling somewhere uncomfortable, meeting people who are not like you. It changes the length of the year you will remember, which is arguably the one that counts.

There is one further consolation in the research, and it is unexpected. Studies of people in their seventies and eighties find that the acceleration slows, and for some it reverses. One possibility is that retirement removes routine; another is that people who know their time is limited begin, consciously or not, to pay attention to it again. Either way, the years that felt shortest turn out to have been the ones in the middle — the decades when there was, apparently, nothing new to remember.

text: From the base camp on the South Inylchek glacier, Khan Tengri does not look like a mountain so much as a piece of geometry: a near-perfect pyramid of pale rock, 7,010 metres high, standing where the borders of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and China meet. The name means “Lord of the Sky”. The old Kazakh name, Kan Tau, means “Blood Mountain”, and anyone who has stood at the glacier at sunset knows why. For about ten minutes the marble summit turns a deep, luminous red, and then, as if a switch had been thrown, goes grey.

Dana Kasymova had watched that sunset eleven times before she began her attempt. She was thirty-four, a surgeon from Almaty, and she had climbed in the Tien Shan every summer for a decade; Her team was small — herself, her long-time partner Bakhyt, and a Kyrgyz guide called Erlan who had summited eight times — and their plan was conservative. Two weeks acclimatising on lower peaks. Three camps on the classic route up the west ridge. A summit push only if the weather window was clear for at least forty-eight hours.

Everything went to plan until the second camp, at 5,800 metres. Bakhyt had developed a cough on the way up from Camp One. That night it grew wetter, and by morning he was breathing fast, with a faint crackling in his chest that Dana, who had spent her professional life listening to lungs, recognised before she had finished putting the stethoscope to his back. High-altitude pulmonary oedema: fluid leaking into the lungs. There is exactly one treatment, which is to go down. Bakhyt, who could see the summit ridge from the tent, argued. He had, he said, come too far. Erlan looked at Dana, and Dana said no, and the discussion ended.

They roped up in the dark and began to descend the fixed lines, with Bakhyt clipped between them, stopping every fifty metres so that he could breathe. At the top of the steep section above Camp One, he sat down in the snow and said he would rest, and Dana pulled him to his feet. It took nine hours to lose 1,200 metres. By the time they reached the glacier, Bakhyt was coughing pink foam and could not stand unaided. A helicopter from the Kyrgyz side took him to Karakol that afternoon. He was back at work in Almaty within a month, with lungs, the doctors said, that would recover completely.

Dana went back up. This is the detail that troubles people. The weather window was still open; Erlan was willing; the fixed ropes were in place. Two days after putting her partner into a helicopter, she left Camp Two at midnight with a headlamp and a thermos and reached the summit of Khan Tengri at a quarter to nine in the morning, in a wind that made it impossible to stand upright, on a marble ridge where the far side dropped two thousand metres into China. She stayed for four minutes. She has a photograph in which nothing is visible except cloud and the edge of her own glove.

Was it the right decision? She thinks so, and she also thinks the question is the wrong one. The decision that mattered, she says, was the one at Camp Two, and it was not a hard decision at all: the medicine was unambiguous and the mountain was irrelevant. What was hard was saying it aloud to a friend who wanted to hear something else. Summit fever — the narrowing of judgement that makes climbers continue when every fact says stop — is usually described as a failure of the individual. In her experience it is a failure of the group: everyone waits for someone else to be the one who says no.

She went back to Khan Tengri the following year, with Bakhyt. They climbed to Camp Two together, looked at the summit ridge for a long time, and came down. It was, she says, the best day she has spent on that mountain.

Wax cylinders were the recording medium of the period.
The recording was attributed to a man who had never played it.
An ethnographer travelled the steppe with a phonograph in 1936.

The discrepancy between the label and the sound was the first clue.

The aim was to restore the name to the recording.

text: The email arrived at the Kurmangazy Conservatory in Almaty in November, from an archivist in St Petersburg. A collection of wax cylinders, recorded in Kazakhstan in 1936 by a Soviet ethnographic expedition, had been digitised as part of a preservation project. Would the conservatory like copies? Aigul, who taught the history of dombra music, replied within the hour. The files came a week later: forty-one tracks, each a kuy — an instrumental piece for the two-stringed dombra — with a typed list giving the title, the performer and the district. It was the seventh track that stopped her.

The title was one she knew, a western Kazakh kuy in the fast, driving tokpe style, and the list attributed it to a well-known male performer from the Atyrau region whose recordings from the 1950s she had heard many times. But the playing was wrong. Not worse — if anything, better — but wrong for him: the ornaments in the left hand were not his ornaments, the tempo breathed differently, and at the return of the main theme there was a fingering that she associated with a different lineage entirely, a school of players from the lower Ural river who taught a particular way of sliding into the note.

A discrepancy on a 1936 label is hardly unusual. But the expedition's field notebooks had also been digitised, and in them, against the date and district of the seventh recording, the ethnographer had written a different name: a woman's, with a note in pencil that had later been crossed out. The crossing-out was in a different ink. Somebody, at some point after the expedition, had decided that the recording should belong to a man.

Finding out who the woman was took most of a winter. The name, Zhamal, was common; the surname was smudged. Aigul wrote to the district archive in Atyrau, and finally to the great-nephew of the male performer, an engineer in Astana who was at first defensive and then, as she played him the recording over the phone, silent. He had grown up, he said, with the kuy. His great-uncle had always said he learned it from “a woman on the Ural who played better than any of us,” and that she had refused to be recorded by the Soviets because her husband was in trouble with the authorities and she did not want her name in a state document. She had played for the expedition on condition of anonymity. The ethnographer had honoured it in the notebook, then reconsidered and the safest name available was the young man who had been standing beside her.

The engineer had a name and a village. Aigul went there in April, when the road was passable, and found the house, and a granddaughter in her seventies who kept, wrapped in a cloth in a cupboard, a dombra with a repaired neck. The granddaughter did not play. But she remembered that her grandmother had, and that she had done so only at home, in the evenings, and that there had been a particular piece she played when she was angry. Aigul asked whether she might play it on the old instrument. The granddaughter listened to the first phrase, went to the window, and stood there until it ended.

The conservatory has now issued the recordings with a corrected list. The seventh kuy is attributed to Zhamal Sarsenova, performer, with a note explaining the history of the label, and the male performer's name appears where it belongs, on the tracks he actually played, which are very fine. The man who received the credit was seventeen at the time and, by every account, never claimed it.

Aigul is often asked whether it matters, ninety years on, whose fingers were on the strings. The kuy is still played; students learn it from her, and she teaches the fingering exactly as it is on the cylinder. For decades they were told they were learning it from a man. They were learning it from a woman on the Ural who played when she was angry, and who was, it turns out, angry enough to play it perfectly.

words.ex: The eruption of Tambora was the largest in recorded history.

text: In April 1815, on the island of Sumbawa in what is now Indonesia, a mountain called Tambora blew itself apart. The eruption was the largest in recorded history — roughly ten times the size of Krakatoa's in 1883 — and it was heard two thousand kilometres away, where the governor of Java assumed it was cannon fire and sent troops to investigate. The mountain lost more than a kilometre of its height. Around twelve thousand people on the island were killed outright, and tens of thousands more died in the famine that followed on Sumbawa and the neighbouring islands.

Tambora had thrown an enormous quantity of sulphur into the stratosphere, where it formed a fine haze of droplets that reflected sunlight back into space. By the summer of 1816 the average temperature of the Northern Hemisphere had fallen by about a degree. In New England it snowed in June. Frost killed the crops in July and again in August. In Europe the summer was not merely cold but dark and endlessly wet; in Switzerland the harvest failed so completely that people ate moss and boiled the leather of their shoes. It was, across the Atlantic world, “the year without a summer”, and nobody knew why.

The connection to a volcano on the other side of the planet would not be made for more than a century. In 1816 the explanations were closer to hand: sunspots, which were unusually visible that year; the wrath of God; and, in the United States, the theory that Benjamin Franklin's lightning rods had upset the balance of the atmosphere. Grain prices in Europe doubled and tripled. Tens of thousands of Germans and Swiss emigrated, many of them to America, and in America itself the ruined farmers of New England moved west, into Ohio and Indiana. The famine in China's Yunnan province, which lasted three years, pushed farmers into growing opium instead of rice.

The gloom entered literature. In June 1816 a group of English writers, trapped indoors by the incessant rain at a villa on Lake Geneva, passed the time by inventing ghost stories. One of them, Mary Shelley, aged eighteen, began the story that became Frankenstein. Lord Byron, looking out at the dark sky, wrote a poem called “Darkness” which begins: “I had a dream, which was not all a dream. The bright sun was extinguished.”

The most unexpected consequence was mechanical. With the harvests gone, there was no oats and no hay, and across Europe horses starved or were slaughtered for food. A German forester named Karl Drais, who could no longer afford to feed a horse, began to think about how a person might travel faster than walking without one. In 1817 he produced a two-wheeled wooden machine that the rider pushed along with the feet: the Laufmaschine, or “running machine”. It had no pedals — those came fifty years later — but it had the essential idea, and the bicycle descends from it directly. The most efficient vehicle ever built by humans was, in this reading, a response to a shortage of horse feed caused by an Indonesian volcano.

It was an American climate scientist, William Humphreys, who in 1920 first proposed that volcanic dust could cool the planet, and only ice-core studies in the second half of the twentieth century identified the sulphur layer of 1815 and gave the year without a summer its cause. Tambora is the closest thing history offers to an experiment in changing the temperature of the whole planet by a single degree, and its results are studied by people trying to imagine what a change of two or three degrees in the other direction might do.

On Sumbawa, the mountain has been quiet for two centuries. A village that was buried in the eruption is being excavated by archaeologists, who have found its inhabitants where the ash caught them, in a moment that in Indonesia was simply a catastrophe and, on the far side of the world, was the beginning of a very strange year.

text: At 4:10 in the afternoon on 14 August 2003, the lights went out across a region of North America stretching from Michigan to Massachusetts and north into Ontario. Fifty-five million people lost power. In New York the subway stopped between stations and thousands of people walked home across the Brooklyn Bridge in the heat. Nearly a hundred power stations shut down within minutes of each other. It was the largest blackout in the history of the continent, and its origin was a tree in Ohio and a bug in a piece of software that nobody had known was there.

The North American grid is sometimes described as the largest machine ever built: thousands of kilometres of lines, hundreds of stations and millions of transformers, all in balance. Electricity cannot be stored in any quantity, so what is generated must equal what is consumed, second by second, across the whole network. The system copes with the loss of any single component — a line, a station — by redistributing the load. That is its strength and its weakness, because a load that is redistributed onto lines that are already hot can push them past their limits, and their failure redistributes still more.

The physical story began just after two o'clock, when a 345,000-volt transmission line owned by FirstEnergy, an Ohio utility, sagged in the afternoon heat. A hot, heavily loaded line expands and droops, and this one drooped into a tree that should have been trimmed and had not been. The line short-circuited and switched itself off. The load shifted to neighbouring lines, which grew hotter, sagged further and, over the next hour and a half, touched trees of their own. By half past three, three major lines were down and the remaining ones were carrying far more than they were built for.

None of this was visible to the people whose job it was to see it. FirstEnergy's control room ran on a system from General Electric, and at 2:14 that afternoon its alarm function had stopped working. The cause, discovered weeks later, was a race condition: two parts of the program had tried to update the same piece of data at the same moment, and the alarm process locked up while waiting for a resource that the other process was holding. No alarm sounded because the alarm system was frozen, and the backup that should have reported the freeze had also failed. For more than an hour the operators watched a picture of a grid that no longer existed. When a neighbouring control centre phoned to ask why lines were tripping in Ohio, the FirstEnergy operators, looking at their screens, said that nothing was wrong.

At 4:05 the failures escaped Ohio. In the space of about seven minutes, a cascade of automatic disconnections rolled through Michigan, across Ontario, into New York and New England. Power that had been flowing east reversed and surged west. By 4:13 it was over, and the cities were silent.

The official investigation, published the following year, ran to over two hundred pages and listed the failures with the flat, cumulative rhythm of such reports: the trees, the software, the absence of a working backup, and above all a culture in which each small failure had been tolerated because nothing had gone wrong before. New rules followed: mandatory tree-trimming, independent monitoring, a fixed bug. Engineers took a different lesson. The blackout had not been caused by any one of those things. It had been caused by all of them at once, lining up in an order nobody had imagined.

The grid has grown more complex since 2003, not less and the engineers who keep it running speak of that August afternoon the way pilots speak of certain crashes: as the event that revealed what the machine was actually like. It is very large, very reliable, and balanced, at every moment, on a set of assumptions that a single tree can test.

text: It is about four millimetres across, transparent, and shaped like a tiny bell with a red stomach visible through the glass. Turritopsis dohrnii lives in warm seas around the world. Then it gets hurt, or hungry, or old — and it does something that no other animal is known to do. It goes back to the beginning.

The life of a typical jellyfish runs in one direction. A fertilised egg becomes a larva, which settles on a rock and grows into a polyp, a small stalk-like creature that looks more like a plant than an animal. The polyp buds off tiny jellyfish, which grow into adults, reproduce and die. Turritopsis follows the same path — until something goes wrong. Under stress, the adult jellyfish sinks to the sea floor, draws its tentacles into its body, and collapses into a shapeless blob of cells. Over the following days the blob reorganises itself and becomes, once again, a polyp, which in due course buds off new jellyfish. The animal has not reproduced. It has, in the language of the biologists who study it, reverted.

What makes this possible is a process called transdifferentiation. The cells of an adult animal are specialised: a muscle cell, a nerve cell, a stinging cell, each committed to one function. In Turritopsis, under the right conditions, those cells abandon their specialities and become something else — muscle turning into nerve, nerve into skin — as the animal rebuilds itself from the material it already has. A jellyfish that reverted, grew up, reverted again and grew up again would be, in the strict sense, biologically immortal: not incapable of dying, but incapable of dying of age.

The discovery was made almost by accident. In 1988 a German biology student named Christian Sommer, collecting specimens off the coast of Italy, kept some Turritopsis in a dish and noticed, to his confusion, that they seemed to be getting younger. Since then the animal has been studied most persistently by Shin Kubota, a Japanese marine biologist at Kyoto University, who has kept colonies in dishes in his laboratory for decades, feeding them by hand, and who has watched a single colony revert and regrow more than a dozen times. He is said to sing to them.

Most biologists are more cautious, for several reasons. Reversion has been reliably observed in the laboratory, but almost never in the wild, where a stressed jellyfish is far more likely to be eaten than to complete its transformation: immortality in principle is not much use to an animal four millimetres long in a sea full of predators. The genetics are only beginning to be understood; a 2022 study identified a set of genes involved in DNA repair and cell renewal that are unusually active in Turritopsis. And the animal is, in most respects, extremely simple: it has no brain, no heart and no blood, and a body that is mostly water. It can afford to dissolve and rebuild itself. We cannot.

What Turritopsis has certainly achieved is a quiet conquest of the oceans. Originally described from the Mediterranean, it now turns up in the Atlantic, the Pacific and the Caribbean, and genetic studies suggest that ships have carried it around the world in their ballast tanks — enormous volumes of seawater taken on for stability and pumped out at the next port. Its ability to survive stress by shrinking into a polyp makes it an ideal stowaway. It is, in this sense, one of the most successful animals on Earth, and almost nobody has ever seen one.

There is a temptation, which journalists rarely resist, to make the jellyfish a symbol of something: of eternal youth, of the ocean's secrets, of what medicine will one day achieve. The animal itself offers no such thing. It is a small bell of tissue that, when the world becomes unbearable, folds itself up and starts again — which, as strategies go, is not the worst one available.

She had to prioritise calls by the height of the water.
Her job was to reassure people she could not see.
Composure is the only tool a dispatcher really has.
In the aftermath, nobody asked about the rule.

text: The call centre of the emergency service in Aktobe is a room without windows, which Saule Zhaksybekova has always considered a design flaw. On the night of 5 April 2024 everyone knew what the weather was doing. The Ilek river, swollen by a winter's snow melting in three days of unseasonal warmth, had broken its banks the previous afternoon, and by midnight the water was rising through the low districts of the city.

She had been a dispatcher for nine years. The job, as she describes it, consists of being the calmest person in a conversation in which the other person has every reason not to be. You answer, you establish where they are, you find out what is wrong, you send what can be sent, and you end the call, because the next call is waiting and the protocol says four minutes. She had done this with car crashes, heart attacks and house fires. She had not done it with a flood, and nobody in the room had, because there had not been one like it in living memory.

The calls that night did not fit the protocol. They came from people on the roofs of single-storey houses in the districts along the river, in the dark, with water at the level of their windows. The boats — the service had eleven, and the army sent more — were reaching them, but not fast enough, and someone had to decide who was reached first. She learned to ask two questions before any other: how high is the water, and are there children. She learned that people on the phone will tell you the truth about the second and lie about the first.

At around two in the morning she took a call from a woman named Bakhyt, seventy-one, alone in a house on the edge of the flooded zone, with water knee-deep in the kitchen and rising. There was a boat perhaps forty minutes away and eleven calls ahead of her. Saule gave her the standard instructions — highest room, warmest clothes, phone charged, do not enter the water — and reached for the button that ends a call. Then she did not press it. She cannot fully explain it; the woman's voice, she says, had the particular steadiness of someone who is very frightened and has decided not to say so. Saule stayed on the line. She stayed for fifty-three minutes, which is thirteen times the protocol, while a colleague quietly took over her queue.

They talked about nothing. Bakhyt's grandchildren in Astana; the price of meat; a neighbour's dog howling at the water from a roof. Every few minutes Saule asked her to describe where the water was, and every few minutes it was higher: the second stair, the third stair. At 2:51 the boat arrived. Saule heard the men shouting, heard the phone put down on a table, and then the line went dead because the phone had been left behind in the house.

In the aftermath there was a review, as there always is. Across the west of the country over a hundred thousand people had been evacuated, in the worst floods for eighty years. Saule's fifty-three-minute call was in the logs, and she waited to be asked about it. She was not. Her supervisor mentioned, some weeks later and without looking up from his screen, that the protocol was a guideline for ordinary nights and that he had not been aware of any ordinary nights that April.

She has kept the job. Bakhyt sent, through the service, a bag of kurt and a note that Saule keeps in the drawer of her console and declines to quote, except for the last line, which says that she would like, one day, to hear the voice again in person, with tea. But the number is in the system, Saule says, and she knows exactly where the water was.

words.ex: The stones functioned as a currency for centuries.
The stone was quarried on an island four hundred kilometres away.
The whole island functioned as a living ledger.
A stone's value depended on its provenance.
A transaction changed the owner, not the location.
Iron tools caused a kind of inflation.
Ownership rested on consensus rather than possession.
All money is an abstraction agreed upon by a community.

text: On the island of Yap, in the western Pacific, there is a coin the size of a car. It stands at the side of a path, a disc of grey limestone with a hole through the middle, and it has not moved in more than a century. It is worth, by local agreement, a great deal, and its owner lives on the other side of the island and has never touched it. To a visiting economist, this arrangement is either absurd or the most honest description of money ever produced.

The stones are called rai, and there are thousands of them on Yap, from the size of a plate to the size of a small room. What makes them remarkable is not the material — limestone is common enough — but where it comes from. There is no limestone on Yap. Every rai was quarried on the island of Palau, four hundred kilometres away across open ocean, and brought back by canoe. For centuries this was the most dangerous activity a Yapese man could undertake. A rai's value depended less on its size than on its provenance. A large, well-carved stone with a boring history was worth less than a small one with a good story.

Because the stones were too heavy to move, they were simply not moved. When a rai changed hands the transaction was announced, everybody remembered it, and the stone stayed exactly where it was, now belonging to someone else. Ownership was a fact held in common by the community rather than a matter of physical possession. The whole island functioned, in effect, as a single ledger.

The most famous illustration of this is a stone that nobody has seen for generations. According to a story recorded by an American anthropologist in the early twentieth century, a particularly large rai was being brought back from Palau when a storm struck, and the crew, to save themselves, cut it loose. It sank in deep water. When the survivors reached Yap, they described the stone, its size and its quality, and the community agreed that it was as valid a rai as any on land — its being at the bottom of the sea was merely an inconvenience. Economists love this stone. It appears in textbooks as a demonstration that money does not need to exist physically in order to work; it needs only to be agreed upon.

The stones also demonstrate what happens when that agreement is disturbed. In the 1870s an Irish-American sailor named David O'Keefe was shipwrecked on Yap and saw an opportunity. He returned with a ship and iron tools, and offered to quarry and transport rai in exchange for coconut products, which he sold in Asia. The result was a flood of new stones — larger, smoother, and produced without danger. The Yapese responded exactly as an economist would predict: the O'Keefe stones were valued far below the old ones, because everybody knew how easily they had been obtained. A century before the term existed, the island had experienced inflation, and had discounted the currency accordingly.

Rai are no longer used for everyday purchases; Yap, a state of the Federated States of Micronesia, uses the US dollar for those. But the stones are still owned, still occasionally transferred at weddings and in settlements between families, and still not moved. Visitors are shown the “stone money banks” — rows of rai along village paths — and are asked, firmly, not to sit on them.

The lesson that economists draw from Yap is usually about the nature of money: that a dollar is, like a rai, valuable because a community has agreed that it is, and for no other reason. That is true. But the islanders themselves might draw a different one. What the stones record is not wealth but history and a society that keeps its history in the open, along the paths where everybody walks, has perhaps understood something that societies with more portable money have not.
